title: Words in Context
kicker: American Diploma · Digital SAT · Craft and Structure
summary: How to choose the most logical and precise word and how to find what a word most nearly means: a seven-step method, the classic traps, four worked examples and a 12-question quiz.

blocks.text: Words in Context questions test whether you can choose — or understand — the exact word an academic writer needs. They look like vocabulary questions, but they are really **logic questions**: the passage always contains a clue that tells you what the missing word must mean. Find the clue, and the answer follows.
What this question type tests

Words in Context is one of the three question types in the **Craft and Structure** domain (about 28% of the scored Reading and Writing questions, 13–15 questions). In each module these questions **usually** come first. Each one has a short passage (25–150 words) and four choices. You will see two forms:

rows: "Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?"
The passage has a blank (______). You choose the word that fits the meaning, the logic and the tone of the passage.
"As used in the text, what does the word "X" most nearly mean?"
One word in the passage is named. You choose the meaning it has in this sentence — often not its most common meaning.

blocks.text: The blank form is much more common. Both forms are solved with the same method, because in both you must decide what meaning the context needs **before** you look at the choices.
The method, step by step

items: **Read the whole passage.** The clue is often in the sentence after the blank, or after a colon or dash.
**Cover the choices.** Do not look at them yet — they are written to distract you.

**Find the clue.** Look for a restatement (colon, dash, "that is", "in other words"), a contrast (although, but, however, yet, while, despite, rather than, not … but), a cause or result (because, so, therefore), or an example that describes the missing idea.
**Predict your own word.** Any simple word is fine: "careful", "proved", "old-fashioned". For the meaning form, cover the named word and put your own word in its place.
**Check the charge (+ / − / neutral).** Is the missing word positive, negative or neutral? Cross out every choice with the wrong charge.

**Check precision and register.** Among the choices left, which one means **exactly** your prediction — the right strength, the right kind of meaning, a natural academic combination with the words around it?
**Plug it back in.** Read the sentence with your answer. It must be logical and must agree with the clue.

rows: colon (:), dash (—), that is, in other words, namely
The blank means the same as the words after the signal.
although, but, however, yet, while, despite, rather than, not … but, instead
The blank means the opposite of the other half.
because, since, so, therefore, as a result
The blank must logically cause, or follow from, the other part.
for example, such as, indeed, in fact
The examples describe the blank; generalize from them.

blocks.title: القاعدة الذهبية
blocks.text: غطّي الاختيارات، ودوّر على "الكلمة الدليل" في النص (زي : أو — أو although أو but). اكتب كلمة من عندك بالمعنى المطلوب، حدّد هل هي إيجابية ولا سلبية، وبعدين اختار الكلمة اللي معناها مضبوط بالظبط، مش الكلمة اللي شكلها صعب أو اللي سمعتها في النص.
Precision: the difference between "close" and "exact"
Often two or three choices have the right charge. The test then checks **precision**. Ask three questions:

items: **Is the strength right?** "Critical" and "hostile" are both negative, but "hostile" is much stronger. If the passage describes polite doubts, "hostile" is too strong.
**Is it the right kind of meaning?** "Sparse" and "brief" both suggest "not much", but "brief" is about time or length, "sparse" about how thinly something is spread.

**Does it fit the words around it (register and collocation)?** Academic writers say "data **support** a claim" and "researchers **posit** a mechanism", not "data **cheer** a claim". The right word sounds natural in formal English.

rows: "Refute" is the precise academic verb for proving a claim wrong.
Her tone was **angry** toward the policy.
Her tone was **skeptical** toward the policy.
If she only asks questions and doubts the evidence, "angry" is the wrong intensity.
"Cheap" can suggest poor quality; "economical" means using resources well.
Collocation: you propose (or posit) a model; you tell a story.

blocks.text: The meaning form: beware the common meaning

When the stem asks what a word "most nearly means", the word chosen almost always has **several meanings**, and the most common one is usually a trap. Example: "The engineers will **address** the overheating problem first." Here address means "deal with", not "speak to an audience" and not "the place where someone lives".

rows: limit or add conditions to (qualify a claim)

blocks.text: Worked examples

**Example 1.** "Although the novelist's early stories were praised for their long, decorative sentences, her later work is strikingly ______: she uses short sentences, few adjectives and almost no description of setting."
Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?   A) spare   B) ornate   C) obscure   D) hostile

**Clue:** "although" (contrast with "decorative") + the colon (restatement: short sentences, few adjectives). **Prediction:** "plain, simple". **Answer: A) spare** — using no more words than needed. **B) ornate** is the opposite trap: it describes her early style. **C) obscure** (hard to understand) is a near-synonym trap: short, simple sentences are not hard to understand, and nothing in the text says the work is unclear. **D) hostile** has the wrong kind of meaning: it describes an attitude toward someone, not a writing style.
**Example 2.** "The committee's response to the proposal was ______: members agreed that the idea had some merit but asked for two more years of data before they would support it."
Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?   A) enthusiastic   B) hostile   C) cautious   D) indifferent

**Clue:** the colon explains the response: some approval + a request for more data. **Prediction:** "careful, not sure yet" (neutral). **Answer: C) cautious.** **A) enthusiastic** is the wrong intensity — far too positive for "some merit". **B) hostile** is the opposite charge: they found merit. **D) indifferent** means not caring, but a committee that asks for two more years of data clearly cares (half-right: they did not support it yet, but not from lack of interest).
**Example 3.** "The historian's account of the revolt is unusually __sound__: each claim is supported by letters, tax records or court documents from the period."
As used in the text, what does the word "sound" most nearly mean?   A) noisy   B) reliable   C) healthy   D) deep

**Clue:** the colon — every claim is backed by documents. **Prediction:** "trustworthy". **Answer: B) reliable.** **A) noisy** is the common-meaning trap (sound as noise). **C) healthy** comes from "safe and sound" — a real meaning of the word, but it describes people, not historical accounts (secondary-meaning trap). **D) deep** comes from "a sound sleep" — again a real meaning in the wrong context.

**Example 4.** "Rather than simply recording how coral reefs lose their color during marine heat waves, ecologist Dina Farouk set out to ______ the process: she identified the specific chemical signals that cause corals to expel the tiny algae living in their tissues."
Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?   A) document   B) elucidate   C) reverse   D) publicize

**Clue:** "rather than simply recording" (contrast) + colon (she found the cause). **Prediction:** "explain how it works". **Answer: B) elucidate** — to make clear, to explain. **A) document** is a near-synonym of "record", which is exactly what the contrast says she went beyond (opposite trap). **C) reverse** is not supported: finding the cause is not the same as undoing the process (too extreme). **D) publicize** (make widely known) has nothing to do with identifying chemical signals (off-topic).

blocks.title: Classic traps
items: **Secondary or common meaning** — a real meaning of the word, but not the one this sentence uses (sound = noisy; check = examine).
**Near-synonym** — almost right, but the wrong kind of meaning (obscure for spare; document for elucidate).
**Wrong intensity** — the right direction but too strong or too weak (hostile for skeptical; enthusiastic for cautious).
**Wrong charge** — positive when the context is negative, or the reverse.
**Hard-word bait** — a difficult, impressive word that you do not fully know. Never choose a word just because it sounds advanced.
**Word-match** — a choice that echoes another word in the passage but does not fit the blank.

blocks.title: Fast strategy for test day
items: Cover the choices, find the clue (colon, dash, although, but, because), predict in simple words.
Charge first (+/−), then precision (strength, kind of meaning, collocation).
If you know three choices are wrong, choose the fourth — even if you do not know that word.
For "most nearly means": replace the word with each choice and reread; reject the most common meaning unless the context clearly needs it.
Target: 45–70 seconds. These come first in the module — do not overthink them.

blocks.title: لو مش عارف معنى كلمة
blocks.text: مش لازم تعرف كل الكلمات. لو اتأكدت إن 3 اختيارات غلط (معناهم عكس الدليل أو أقوى من اللازم)، يبقى الرابع هو الصح حتى لو أول مرة تشوفه. وفي أسئلة most nearly means، المعنى المشهور للكلمة غالبًا هو الفخ.
Practice
Twelve Words in Context questions in true test format: nine blank questions and three "most nearly means" questions. Use the full method on every item.

blocks.title: Words in Context practice: 12 questions
blocks.intro: Untimed. Cover the choices, find the clue, predict, check charge and precision. Aim for about one minute per question.

questions.p: The volunteers were remarkably ______: despite heavy rain, cold nights and twelve-hour shifts, not one of them left the rescue site before the work was finished.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.e: The colon explains the blank: they stayed despite hardship, so they were determined — "tenacious." "Reluctant" (unwilling) and "fickle" (changing easily) are opposite traps, and "idle" (not working) contradicts twelve-hour shifts.

questions.p: Early reviews of the film were ______, with critics disagreeing sharply: some called it a masterpiece, while others described it as slow and confusing.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.e: Critics disagreed — some positive, some negative — so the reviews were "mixed." "Unanimous" (all agreeing) is the opposite, "glowing" is only half-right (only the positive reviews), and "brief" is about length, not opinion.

questions.p: Before the new battery can be sold, its designers must __address__ the problem of overheating, which caused several prototypes to fail during testing.
questions.q: As used in the text, what does the word "address" most nearly mean?
questions.e: The designers must solve the overheating problem: "deal with." "Give a speech about," "send a letter to" and "find the location of" are common meanings of "address" that do not fit a technical problem (secondary-meaning traps).

questions.p: Because the fossil is only a single damaged tooth, paleontologist Omar Haddad is ______ about identifying it as a new species; he notes that it could also belong to a young individual of a species that is already known.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.e: One damaged tooth and another possible explanation make Haddad careful and unsure: "tentative." "Certain" is the opposite, "indifferent" (not caring) is wrong because he clearly thinks about the question, and "furious" is the wrong kind of meaning.

questions.p: A packaging company claimed that its new plastic breaks down completely within six months. An independent laboratory test, however, ______ that claim: after a full year, samples of the material showed almost no sign of decay.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.e: "However" and the evidence (no decay after a year) show the test weakened the claim: "undermined." "Confirmed" is the opposite trap, and "inspired" and "repeated" do not describe evidence that goes against a claim.

questions.p: In her speech, the minister said she had __entertained__ the idea of extending the school day, but she made no promises and said that teachers and parents would be consulted first.
questions.q: As used in the text, what does the word "entertained" most nearly mean?
questions.e: She thought about the idea without promising anything: "considered." "Amused," "hosted" and "performed for" are common meanings of "entertain" that refer to people or guests, not to ideas (common-meaning traps).

questions.p: The drop in the river's water level was ______ — only a few centimetres over the whole summer — so farmers along its banks noticed no change in their harvests.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.e: The dashes restate the blank: only a few centimetres, with no effect on harvests, means "negligible" (too small to matter). "Catastrophic" and "dramatic" are the wrong intensity, and "sudden" contradicts "over the whole summer."

questions.p: Ancient Egyptian builders did not simply place stones wherever they fit; they ______ the position of each block using knotted cords, wooden measuring tools and careful observation of the stars.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.e: The contrast with placing stones at random, plus the measuring tools, shows careful planning: "calculated." "Guessed" is the opposite of using measuring tools, "ignored" makes no sense, and "decorated" is about appearance, not position (off-topic).

questions.p: Many readers find the novel's ending __flat__: after three hundred pages of rising tension, the main conflict is settled in a single, unremarkable paragraph.
questions.q: As used in the text, what does the word "flat" most nearly mean?
questions.e: An unremarkable ending after so much tension lacks excitement: "dull." "Level" (a flat surface), "punctured" (a flat tire) and "fixed" (a flat price) are real meanings of "flat" that do not fit a story (secondary-meaning traps).

questions.p: Although critics at first dismissed the architect's use of mud brick as ______, her buildings are now praised as a modern, energy-efficient way to keep homes cool in hot climates.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.e: "Although" sets up a contrast with "modern" and "energy-efficient," so the critics first saw mud brick as old-fashioned: "outdated." "Innovative" and "efficient" repeat today's praise (opposite trap), and "durable" is positive and unrelated to the contrast.

questions.p: Geologist Lina Mostafa's data do not merely suggest that the two volcanoes share a source of magma. By showing that rock samples from both sites contain the same rare chemical signature, her analysis ______ that connection.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.e: "Not merely suggest" signals something stronger than a suggestion, and matching chemical evidence proves the link: "establishes." "Questions" is the opposite, "imagines" is weaker than "suggest" (wrong intensity), and "hides" makes no sense.

questions.p: Strict new limits on fishing helped __check__ the decline of the sardine population, which had been falling steadily for more than a decade.
questions.q: As used in the text, what does the word "check" most nearly mean?
questions.e: Fishing limits helped halt the falling population: "stop." "Examine," "mark" (a check mark) and "test" are common meanings of "check" that do not describe what limits do to a decline (common-meaning traps).

blocks.title: Remember
items: Two forms: the blank ("most logical and precise word") and "as used in the text … most nearly means".
The passage always contains a clue: restatement (: — that is), contrast (although, but, however), cause (because, so) or examples.
Predict your own word before reading the choices, then check charge (+/−) and precision (strength, kind of meaning, collocation).
In "most nearly means" questions, the most common meaning of the word is usually the trap.
Eliminate confidently: if three choices are wrong, the fourth is right even if you do not know it.
